method: Clauset, Shalizi and Newman (2009), SIAM Review 51(4), 661-703, fitted with the powerlaw package (Alstott, Bullmore and Plenz 2014)
note: p is the share of synthetic datasets from the fitted model that fit it worse than the data does. p below 0.1 rules the power law out; a large p does not rule it in. R is Vuong's normalised log-likelihood ratio: positive favours the power law, negative the rival, and its p above 0.1 means the two cannot be separated at this sample size.

in_degree.label: Origins per destination (in-degree)
in_degree.verdict: Ruled out on its own terms: a power law above 15 produces a fit this poor in 0% of its own draws. The lognormal describes the same tail better. The exponential cannot be separated from it either way.

out_degree.label: Destinations per origin (out-degree)
out_degree.verdict: Ruled out on its own terms: a power law above 33 produces a fit this poor in 6% of its own draws. That is close to the 0.1 line the convention draws, and with 122 points in the tail it is the weakest kind of rejection. The lognormal and exponential describe the same tail better.

flight_degree.label: Flight partners per country

That is close to the 0.1 line the convention draws, and with 75 points in the tail it is the weakest kind of rejection. The lognormal and exponential cannot be separated from it either way.
